newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Merck describes new painkiller.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Merck describes new painkiller.

text.p: A new painkiller with all the benefits of aspirin or ibuprofen but few of the side-effects could offer safer treatment for arthritis sufferers, one of Merck and Co Inc's top researchers said on Tuesday.

Dr Briggs Morrison described work on two drugs known as COX-2 inhibitors, which mimic the painkilling effects of non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDS) without the bleeding and damage to the stomach and intestines.
NSAIDS such as aspirin, ibuprofen and naproxen are extremely popular and work well against the type of pain seen in arthritis and after minor surgery.

They act on two enzymes known as cyclooxygenase-1 (COX-1) and COX-2. COX-1 is present in virtually all tissues and is involved in a variety of important functions. COX-2 seems to be produced by the body mostly in response to trauma.
This discovery has sent a few drug companies racing to see if they can produce a drug that works only against COX-2.

"The COX-2 inhibitors, we do believe, represent a new direction in pain control," Morrison, associate director of Merck Research Labs in Rahway, New Jersey, told an IBC conference on pain control in London.

He described tests on Merck's two experimental COX-2 inhibitors -- MK966, which is in Phase III trials in people and L-745.337, which seems to be even more selective against COX-2 than MK966 but is still in early stages of testing.
"If you can get a very, very potent compound that gets COX-2 at low doses, then you don't have to worry about the effects on COX-1," Morrison said.

COX inhibitors eventually work against prostaglandins, chemicals that not only cause the pain associated with inflammation but also protect the stomach lining, regulate blood-clotting and balance water and salt in the kidneys.
